issues.title: Later review of storage, release, receptor, reuptake and metabolism dietary candidates
findings: Current Dietary Requirements mainly address dopamine synthesis.

pages.title: Serotonergic Signalling Regulation
pages.review_scope: Dietary Requirements classification on this page. This is not source verification or expert review.

issues.title: Later serotonin-handling steps are not yet assessed as diet
findings: Synthesis-path requirements are listed.
Reuptake and breakdown have not been classified as Dietary Requirements.
issues.section: §3.1 Dietary Requirements — later stages beyond synthesis
issues.description: How serotonin is stored, released, taken back up and broken down is part of the signalling story. Whether those later steps have their own ordinary-diet requirements has not been finished.
issues.decision: Do not add dietary entries for those later steps until they are assessed.

corrections.title: Serotonin is made from tryptophan in two enzyme steps
findings: Serotonin helps set mood stability, inhibition and behavioural regulation.
The first synthesis step needs iron and tetrahydrobiopterin; the second needs PLP.
Competitive amino-acid transport is an earlier step, not serotonin signalling.
corrections.description: Tryptophan hydroxylase converts tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan and needs iron and tetrahydrobiopterin. A second enzyme then uses vitamin B6 (as PLP) to make serotonin. That is biological chemistry, not a mood or ADHD treatment.
corrections.decision: Keep synthesis chemistry separate from dietary dosing and from meal-level amino-acid transport.

corrections.title: Tryptophan, iron and vitamin B6 are synthesis requirements, not serotonin doses
findings: Tryptophan is required as the serotonin starting material.
Iron and PLP are required enzyme helpers.
Dietary protein is not a separate serotonin requirement beyond the amino-acid supply mechanism.
corrections.description: Tryptophan is the starting material. Iron and PLP are cofactors. Vitamin B6 is the dietary route to PLP. Tetrahydrobiopterin is made in the body. Extra intake has not been shown to raise brain serotonin or improve mood when status is already adequate.
corrections.decision: List tryptophan, iron, PLP and vitamin B6 as Dietary Requirements. Keep tetrahydrobiopterin as an endogenous cofactor. Do not list dietary protein on this mechanism.

pages.title: Acetylcholine Synthesis Support
pages.review_scope: Foundational synthesis chemistry, Dietary Requirements, biochemical participants, intervention dominance, connections and complete Key Constraint applicability. Sources were checked; this is not expert peer review.

corrections.title: Acetylcholine synthesis inputs and shared one-carbon constraint corrected
findings: Choline transport and the choline-acetyl-CoA reaction are the defining synthesis steps.
Phosphatidylcholine provides choline; vitamin B5 supports acetyl-CoA provision through coenzyme A.
Animal models support a constrained relationship between one-carbon status and the brain choline-acetylcholine resource.
corrections.description: Acetylcholine synthesis uses choline and acetyl-CoA after choline enters cholinergic nerve endings. Phosphatidylcholine can provide choline, and vitamin B5 supports the coenzyme A route to acetyl-CoA. One-carbon impairment can constrain the shared choline resource, but extra intake has not been shown here to raise human brain acetylcholine.
corrections.decision: Keep choline as the Direct substrate, list phosphatidylcholine as its Derived provision route, list acetyl-CoA and its vitamin B5 precursor in the biochemical inventory, and map BRS2(KC1) without copying its nutrient or food list.

limitations: No direct human ordinary-diet study establishes increased brain acetylcholine synthesis or cognitive benefit.
Pantothenate modulation evidence is preclinical and involves chronic ethanol-associated severe depletion.
One-carbon applicability is supported by a preclinical mechanistic chain rather than a direct human synthesis-flux assay.

corrections.title: Betaine-dependent remethylation constraint reassessed
findings: Controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced post-load homocysteine-handling reserve in clinically depleted participants.
The response returned to baseline after choline repletion while folate remained adequate.
Rat studies add hepatic-betaine rescue and specific BHMT-inhibition evidence in the same pathway direction.

Vitamin B12 remains outside canonical methyl-donor-pool membership, and the methionine–cysteine pool is not mapped to this mechanism.

pages.review_scope: §4 Emerging Biological Supports: creatine, SAMe and named methyl-cycle adjuncts. Core Nutritional Requirements and PM mappings were not reopened.

corrections.title: Emerging methyl-resource supports reassessed
findings: SAMe increases circulating SAM exposure but does not restore dietary donor inputs or establish general tissue methylation benefit.
Creatine suppresses endogenous creatine synthesis, but human evidence does not show redistribution of spared methyl resources or a methyl-sparing functional benefit.
Riboflavin increased plasma SAM in a small MTHFR 677TT intervention, supporting genotype-conditioned assessment rather than a general recommendation.
Each retained support has a five-field traceability disclosure while remaining separate from Core Nutritional Requirements.
corrections.description: The former wording rejected candidates for not being indispensable nutrients, although §4 asks whether an intervention can support the pool or related regulatory capacity under defined conditions.
corrections.decision: Prioritise SAMe conditionally and riboflavin narrowly for MTHFR 677TT; retain creatine as an emerging demand-reduction support while leaving downstream methyl redistribution and benefit unresolved.

limitations: Creatine suppression of endogenous synthesis has not been shown to redistribute methyl resources to other pathways in humans.
SAMe plasma exposure does not establish intracellular or tissue-specific methylation benefit, and long-term safety evidence is limited.
The riboflavin SAM response is based on a small MTHFR 677TT genotype-selected intervention.

pages.title: Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation
pages.review_scope: Source check of Houghton 2016, Verlaet 2018, Costa 2026, Riedl 2009, and Wise 2016 for food versus supplement classification, vitamin C, zinc, selenium, dominance, and the repeated-exposure sentence. The 2019 Mocchegiani and Malavolta chapter was not retrieved in full. This is not expert review.

corrections.title: Broccoli sprout homogenate is a food preparation
findings: Riedl 2009 gave healthy adults a broccoli sprout homogenate once a day for three days. The sprouts were blended with water, mixed with daikon sprouts, and held at 37°C so myrosinase could finish forming sulforaphane.
Nasal-cell RNA for phase II enzymes rose. Alfalfa sprout homogenate did not. Nrf2 protein and brain endpoints were not measured.
Wise 2016 gave people with COPD capsules of sulforaphane extracted from broccoli sprouts for four weeks. Lung Nrf2 target-gene expression did not rise.
corrections.description: The admitted practice is a three-day broccoli sprout homogenate prepared with added myrosinase. It is not an ordinary broccoli serving and not a sulforaphane capsule.
corrections.decision: Admit the homogenate under Food Preparation and Delivery. Do not admit a sulforaphane supplement.

corrections.title: Vitamin C is not a constraint on this activation step
findings: Verlaet lists vitamin C as a water-soluble non-enzymatic antioxidant.
Houghton reports ascorbic acid as a much weaker NQO1 inducer than sulforaphane, and treats ascorbate as a direct antioxidant used up in the reaction.
Verlaet places zinc on copper-zinc superoxide dismutase and selenium on glutathione peroxidase.
corrections.description: Vitamin C stays a direct antioxidant in the sources. It is not shown to constrain Nrf2 activation. Zinc and selenium are cofactors of downstream enzymes, not of the switch.
corrections.decision: Remove the vitamin C key-constraint disclosure. Do not admit zinc or selenium as requirements of Nrf2 activation.

corrections.title: Diet is not established as the principal route
findings: Houghton says phase II enzymes can last for days, so induction need not be continuous. It does not compare repeated exposure with a single dose.
The only admitted intervention effect is the three-day homogenate. Absence of another admitted route does not establish dietary dominance.
corrections.description: A food preparation changed nasal defence-gene RNA. That does not make diet the principal route. The sources do not show that repeated exposure matters more than a single dose.
corrections.decision: Use Diet-Supported. Place the admitted food-preparation practice at 1.1, because no direct dietary requirement is established. Remove the repeated-exposure claim.

limitations: The admitted practice is a three-day myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate and nasal enzyme RNA, not brain Nrf2 or an ordinary broccoli serving.
A four-week broccoli-sprout extract capsule did not raise lung Nrf2 target-gene expression in COPD.
